strong_form: For an agent at a local optimum, any move to a higher peak must cross a region of lower payoff, and no information available beforehand can justify making the crossing; so rational, evidence-based decision procedures will never leave local optima, and leaving takes a non-rational commitment ('faith').
weak_form: Leaving a local optimum often needs commitment beyond what current evidence fully warrants, and some optimism or underestimated difficulty can help, as in Hirschman's Hiding Hand.
refuted_if: Showing that decision procedures with exploration that is justified from available information (value-of-information calculations, UCB/optimism-in-the-face-of-uncertainty, simulated annealing schedules, neutral-network drift) reliably escape local optima with provable guarantees.
synonyms: optimism in the face of uncertainty

prior_art.citation: Hiding hand principle (Hirschman 1967): underestimating difficulty lets projects begin
Flyvbjerg & Sunstein, The Principle of the Malevolent Hiding Hand
Stochastic Bandits: Optimism in the Face of Uncertainty (UCB regret bounds)
Simulated annealing as principled acceptance of worse moves (gradient-free-optimizers docs)
van Nimwegen & Crutchfield, neutral evolution crosses entropy barriers faster than fitness barriers

strongest_criticism: Decision theory and bandit/optimization theory show that exploration can be justified from available information: the expected value of information and optimistic confidence bounds rationally license moves that lower short-term payoff, with provable regret guarantees. Evolution also crosses valleys blindly, through drift and neutral networks, with no faith involved. What remains true is the weaker point that a specific crossing can't be guaranteed to pay off, which is ordinary decision-making under uncertainty, not a limit of rationality.
